HSTU adds relative positional and temporal bias before pointwise SiLU attention aggregation; deleting events can therefore change content, positional distances, time gaps and evidence quantity simultaneously. The paper explicitly motivates unnormalized aggregation as preserving preference-intensity information from the number of relevant events. A deletion-induced accuracy drop alone cannot establish recent-content dependence. [Original paper](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mlresearch/v235/main/assets/zhai24a/zhai24a.pdf)

Recommended controls, inferred from this architecture: truncate the original chronological history once to the baseline window, then perturb that same window without backfilling older events. Compare recent-k deletion with oldest-k and repeated random-k deletions on identical eligible users, retaining equal lengths. Preserve surviving events’ actual timestamps and timestamp units; keep prediction/query time fixed where used. Report whether positions are compacted or original positional distances are retained. Compacted deletion measures the combined intervention; retaining original distances requires explicit position/bias handling, since inserting padding does not necessarily preserve the intended attention geometry. Keep left padding, causal masking and final-nonpadding readout correct.

For a length-preserving content/order probe, shuffle item identities across fixed timestamp/position slots; leave the final item fixed in one control and include it in another, separating earlier-history effects from the changed readout token. Moving item–timestamp pairs together is a different intervention that changes temporal placement and may violate chronological order. Keep the same trained checkpoint, validation users, targets and candidate sets; report paired HR@10 changes across repeated perturbations. These are proposed diagnostic controls, not deletion/shuffling findings established by the HSTU paper. If the supplied backbone lacks temporal bias, explicitly report that fact rather than inventing timestamp effects.
